title: Bio-inorganic Chemistry Introduction
notes: **Definition:** Bio-inorganic chemistry is the study of the role of metal ions and inorganic elements in biological systems, including their structure, function, and interactions with biomolecules like proteins and nucleic acids.

**Macronutrients (bulk elements):** Na, K, Mg, Ca are required in amounts greater than 100 mg/day. They serve structural and electrochemical roles. Na$^+$ and K$^+$ maintain osmotic balance and nerve impulse transmission. Ca$^{2+}$ is essential for bones, teeth, blood clotting, and muscle contraction.

**Micronutrients (trace elements):** Fe, Cu, Zn, Ni, Co, Cr are required in amounts less than 100 mg/day but are vital for enzyme function. Iron is in haemoglobin and cytochromes. Zinc is in carbonic anhydrase and carboxypeptidase. Copper is in cytochrome c oxidase and tyrosinase.

**Sodium (Na$^+$):** Major extracellular cation. Maintains osmotic pressure and fluid balance. Essential for nerve impulse transmission along the axon. The Na$^+$/K$^+$-ATPase pump maintains the concentration gradient across cell membranes.

**Potassium (K$^+$):** Major intracellular cation. Maintains cell volume and intracellular pH. Essential for heart rhythm — K$^+$ imbalance causes cardiac arrhythmias. Also involved in protein synthesis and enzyme activation.

**Magnesium (Mg$^{2+}$):** Central atom in chlorophyll ($C_{55}H_{72}MgN_4O_5$) in plants, enabling photosynthesis. Activates over 300 enzymes. Essential for ATP function — ATP exists as Mg-ATP complex in biological systems.

**Calcium (Ca$^{2+}$):** Forms the mineral matrix of bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite ($Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2$). Acts as a secondary messenger in cell signaling. Required for blood clotting cascade and muscle contraction (troponin binding).

**Iron (Fe):** Present as Fe$^{2+}$ in haemoglobin (oxygen transport) and myoglobin (oxygen storage). In cytochromes, iron cycles between Fe$^{2+}$ and Fe$^{3+}$ during electron transport in mitochondria. Also in ferritin (iron storage protein).

**Zinc (Zn$^{2+}$):** Catalytic and structural role in over 200 enzymes. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes $CO_2 + H_2O \\\\ightleftharpoons H_2CO_3$ in red blood cells, increasing the rate 10,000-fold. Zinc finger proteins are crucial for DNA binding and gene expression.

**Copper (Cu$^{2+}$/Cu$^{+}$):** Cycles between Cu(I) and Cu(II) in redox reactions. Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV in electron transport) uses copper centers to reduce $O_2$ to $H_2O$. Superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn-SOD) detoxifies superoxide radicals.

**Cobalt (Co$^{2+}$):** Central atom in vitamin B$_{12}$ (cobalamin, $C_{63}H_{88}CoN_{14}O_{14}P$), which is essential for DNA synthesis and nerve function. The cobalt-carbon bond in B$_{12}$ is one of the few natural organometallic bonds.

**Nickel (Ni$^{2+}$):** Present in urease enzyme, which catalyzes hydrolysis of urea: $(NH_2)_2CO + H_2O \\\\ightarrow 2NH_3 + CO_2$. Also in some hydrogenases and carbon monoxide dehydrogenases in microorganisms.
**Chromium (Cr$^{3+}$):** Involved in glucose metabolism as part of glucose tolerance factor (GTF), which enhances insulin action. Cr deficiency leads to impaired glucose tolerance.

**Manganese (Mn$^{2+}$):** Central to the oxygen-evolving complex (OEC) in Photosystem II of plants, which catalyzes water splitting: $2H_2O \\\\ightarrow O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^-$. Also in Mn-superoxide dismutase for antioxidant defense.
confusion: **Trace elements are less important because they are needed in small amounts** — Trace elements like Fe, Zn, and Cu are absolutely essential. Deficiency in any trace element causes severe disease. Iron deficiency causes anaemia; zinc deficiency impairs immune function and growth.

**All metal ions are toxic to living organisms** — While some heavy metals (Hg, Pb, Cd) are toxic, essential metal ions are required for life. The body carefully regulates their concentrations through transport proteins, storage proteins, and excretion mechanisms.

**Calcium is only important for bones** — Calcium serves multiple roles beyond bone structure: it acts as a second messenger in intracellular signaling, triggers muscle contraction by binding troponin, activates blood clotting factors, and regulates neurotransmitter release.

universalFacts: About 25% of all known enzymes require metal ion cofactors for catalytic activity — these are called metalloenzymes.
Haemoglobin contains about 70% of the iron in the human body, with approximately 3 grams of iron bound in roughly 25 trillion red blood cells.
The sodium-potassium pump consumes approximately 20-25% of all ATP produced by a resting human cell, highlighting the energetic cost of maintaining ionic gradients.
Chlorophyll is structurally related to haemoglobin — both contain a porphyrin ring with a metal center (Mg in chlorophyll, Fe in haemoglobin).
Zinc is the second most abundant trace element in the human body (after iron), with about 2-3 grams distributed across all tissues.
